title: Blood and water (John 19:31–37)
hookLine: a spear, and the eyewitness insists: he saw it
last: A DEBT PAID, A VICTORY WON.

lines: THE NARRATOR STEPS INTO THE FRAME.
cards: John usually tells his story in a calm, steady voice. Then, right after the death of Jesus, the narrator does something unusual. He steps almost into the frame and speaks straight to you.
I'm not making this up, he says, in effect. Someone saw it. And he's telling you so that you will believe.
It's like a documentary where the person holding the camera turns it around for a moment.

teach.h: A HIGH DAY: LEGS BROKEN, BUT NOT HIS.
teach.b: It's the day of preparation, and the next day is a Sabbath, a high day. The bodies can't be left on the crosses into it. So the authorities ask Pilate to have the legs broken and the bodies taken down.
Soldiers break the legs of the two men crucified with Jesus. Then they come to him.

teach.h: A SPEAR, AND BLOOD AND WATER.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "But when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was dead already, they brake not his legs: But one of the soldiers with a spear pierced his side, and forthwith came there out blood and water."
Then the unusual line: "And he that saw it bare record, and his record is true: and he knoweth that he saith true, that ye might believe." Bare record means testified.
The Greek verb is martyreo, to bear witness. It's where our word martyr comes from: a martyr was first of all a witness. Why does John stress this so hard?
Some early Christians taught that Jesus only seemed to have a body, and only seemed to die.

teach.h: REAL BODY, REAL DEATH, A REAL WITNESS.
teach.b: Some scholars think John is answering that: real spear, real wound, real death, and someone standing there. John also hears two scriptures. A bone of him shall not be broken: the rule for the Passover lamb.
And from the prophet Zechariah: they shall look on him whom they pierced. Then there's the blood and the water itself.

teach.h: HE THAT SAW IT BARE RECORD.
teach.b: John doesn't explain it. Early church writers like Augustine and John Chrysostom saw in it the two great signs of the church: the water of baptism and the blood of Communion. Others read it as simple evidence of death.
The text leaves it there, with a witness.

how: Some Christians see the blood and water as signs of Communion and baptism, and Catholic devotion to the Sacred Heart and the Divine Mercy image both draw on this moment.

o: to bear witness to what you have seen
to suffer and die for what you believe
to keep a record of the law in writing

games.why: "he that saw it bare record, and his record is true... that ye might believe." the narrator steps into the frame.

practice: Think of someone who told you about something they saw or lived through, a grandparent's war story, a friend's account of how they were treated, a coworker who said something was wrong, and you didn't quite take it in.
Bring their face to mind and hear their words again, slowly, as if they were telling the truth, because they may have been. If you pray, give thanks for them; if not, simply honor them in your mind.

wordCard.voice: Martyreo. The Greek verb meaning to bear witness, the root of our word martyr: what the eyewitness did at the cross.

orig.note: Greek: he has borne witness. from martyreo; the root of the word martyr.

carryVoice: Your line: he who saw it. Someone was standing there, and said so. That's today's walk.
